claim: Alternative isoforms of the DOMINO nucleosome remodeling ATPase, DOM-A and DOM-B, directly specify two distinct multi-subunit complexes.
source: Here we show that alternative isoforms of the DOMINO nucleosome remodeling ATPase, DOM-A and DOM-B, directly specify two distinct multi-subunit complexes.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data showing distinct interactors for DOM-A and DOM-B (Figure 1C, 1D, 1E)

claim: Both DOM-A and DOM-B complexes are necessary for transcriptional regulation but through different mechanisms.
source: Both complexes are necessary for transcriptional regulation but through different mechanisms.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data showing different transcriptional responses upon DOM-A vs DOM-B depletion (Figure 2B, 2C, 2D)

claim: The DOM-B complex incorporates H2A.V genome-wide in an ATP-dependent manner, like the yeast SWR1 complex.
source: The DOM-B complex incorporates H2A.V (the fly ortholog of H2A.Z) genome-wide in an ATP-dependent manner, like the yeast SWR1 complex.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq showing H2A.V loss upon DOM-B depletion (Figure 3B, 3C) and complementation assays showing ATP-dependence (Figure 3E, 3F, 3G)

claim: The DOM-A complex functions as an ATP-independent histone acetyltransferase complex similar to the yeast NuA4, targeting lysine 12 of histone H4.
source: The DOM-A complex, instead, functions as an ATP-independent histone acetyltransferase complex similar to the yeast NuA4, targeting lysine 12 of histone H4.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry showing H4K12ac reduction upon DOM-A depletion (Figure 4A) and complementation assays showing ATP-independence (Figure 4D, 4E)

claim: Drosophila generates functional diversity between SWR1 and NuA4 complexes by alternative splicing of a single gene, while yeast and humans achieve this through gene duplication and paralog specification.
source: In yeast and humans, nucleosome remodeling and histone acetyltransferase complexes originate from gene duplication and paralog specification. Drosophila generates the same diversity by alternative splicing of a single gene.
evidence: Supported by comparison of evolutionary strategies across species (Figure 4F) and citation to known literature on yeast and human systems

claim: DOM-A and DOM-B are identical for the first 2008 amino acids but alternative splicing diversifies their C-termini.
source: The isoforms of the DOMINO ATPase, DOM-A and DOM-B, are identical for the first 2008 amino acids, but alternative splicing diversifies their C-termini (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by schematic representation in Figure 1A showing domain structure

claim: Both DOM-A and DOM-B share an N-terminal HSA domain and a central, INO80-like ATPase domain.
source: Both proteins share an N-terminal HSA domain and a central, INO80-like ATPase domain.
evidence: Supported by domain structure shown in Figure 1A

claim: DOM-A has a longer C-terminus characterized by a SANT domain and a region rich in poly-glutamine stretches (Q-rich).
source: DOM-A has a longer C-terminus characterized by a SANT domain and a region rich in poly-glutamine stretches (Q-rich).
evidence: Supported by domain structure shown in Figure 1A

claim: The shorter C-terminus of DOM-B folds in no predictable manner.
source: The shorter C-terminus of DOM-B, instead, folds in no predictable manner.
evidence: Based on structural prediction analysis

claim: Mass-spectrometry analysis revealed 13 and 12 strongly enriched interactors (FDR < 0.05 and log2 fold-change >0) for DOM-A and DOM-B, respectively.
source: Mass-spectrometry analysis revealed 13 and 12 strongly enriched interactors (FDR < 0.05 and log2 fold-change >0) for DOM-A and DOM-B, respectively (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1

claim: Seven interactors are common between DOM-A and DOM-B and were previously characterized as DOM interactors.
source: Of those, 7 are common between the two isoforms and were previously characterized as DOM interactors (Kusch et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data and citation to previous work

claim: Three proteins that specifically associate with DOM-A (ING3, E(Pc) and TIP60) share extensive homology with the acetyltransferase module of the yeast NuA4 complex.
source: Three of the proteins that specifically associate with DOM-A [ING3, E(Pc) and TIP60] share extensive homology with the acetyltransferase module of the yeast NuA4 complex.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 1D) and homology analysis

claim: NIPPED-A specifically associates with DOM-A.
source: Another component of the yeast NuA4.C, NIPPED-A, specifically associates with DOM-A.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1D

claim: ARP6 and PPS are specific interactors of DOM-B.
source: On the DOM-B side, only ARP6 and PPS appear to be specific interactors of this isoform.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The yeast homolog of ARP6 is essential for H2A.Z remodeling by the SWR1.C.
source: While ARP6 was not described before in Drosophila, its yeast homolog is essential for H2A.Z remodeling by the SWR1.C (Wu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: TIP60 interacts with DOM-A and not with DOM-B.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation confirmed that TIP60 interacts with DOM-A and not with DOM-B (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1E

claim: DOM-A and DOM-B do not interact with each other under stringent conditions.
source: Importantly, the same co-immunoprecipitation showed that DOM-A and DOM-B do not interact with each other under these conditions.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Isoform-specific depletion by RNAi of either DOM variant did not lead to depletion of the other isoform.
source: Isoform-specific depletion by RNA interference (RNAi) of either DOM variant in a Drosophila embryonic cell line did not lead to depletion of the other isoform (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Knock-down of DOM-A (but not DOM-B) led to a strong reduction of TIP60 protein levels.
source: Interestingly, knock-down of DOM-A (but not DOM-B) led to a strong reduction of TIP60 protein levels.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A

claim: tip60 mRNA levels were unchanged upon DOM-A knock-down.
source: tip60 mRNA levels were unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that TIP60 requires DOM-A for stability (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: TIP60 requires DOM-A for stability.
source: tip60 mRNA levels were unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that TIP60 requires DOM-A for stability (Figure 2A).
evidence: Inferred from unchanged mRNA levels but reduced protein levels upon DOM-A knock-down

claim: Most of TIP60 resides in the DOM-A complex in Drosophila cells.
source: This suggests that most of TIP60 resides in the DOM-A complex in Drosophila cells.
evidence: Inferred from TIP60 instability upon DOM-A depletion

claim: Knock-down of either DOM-A, DOM-B, TIP60 or H2A.V individually resulted in significant perturbation of transcription, with notable differences.
source: Knock-down of either DOM-A, DOM-B, TIP60 or H2A.V individually resulted in significant perturbation of transcription, with notable differences (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Principal Components Analysis (PCA) revealed clearly different transcriptional responses upon loss of DOM-A or DOM-B.
source: Principal Components Analysis (PCA) revealed clearly different transcriptional responses upon loss of DOM-A or DOM-B (Figure 2B), which can be visualized by comparing their log2 fold-changes relative to control (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: The correlation value of 0.45 between DOM-A and DOM-B transcriptional effects indicates that many genes are regulated similarly by both ATPases, but a significant number of genes are also differentially affected.
source: The correlation value of 0.45 indicates that many genes are regulated similarly by both ATPases, but a significant number of genes are also differentially affected upon specific depletion of either DOM-A or DOM-B (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: The transcriptional effects of DOM-A knock-down, but not of DOM-B, resemble the ones caused by knock-down of TIP60.
source: As expected, the transcriptional effects of DOM-A knock-down, but not of DOM-B, resemble the ones caused by knock-down of TIP60 (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: Supported by PCA and correlation analysis shown in Figure 2B and 2D

claim: Depletion of H2A.V led to a global reduction of transcription, only observable by normalization to spiked-in D.virilis RNA.
source: Depletion of H2A.V led to a global reduction of transcription, only observable by normalization to spiked-in D.virilis RNA (see methods) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by spike-in normalization analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: The effects of H2A.V depletion were better correlated to DOM-B (r = 0.51) than to DOM-A knock-down (r = 0.25).
source: The effects of H2A.V depletion were better correlated to DOM-B (r = 0.51) than to DOM-A knock-down (r = 0.25) (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: DOM-B depletion caused a strong H2A.V reduction in nuclear extracts.
source: We found a strong H2A.V reduction upon DOM-B depletion (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), while H2A.V mRNA level was unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A

claim: H2A.V mRNA level was unchanged upon DOM-B depletion.
source: We found a strong H2A.V reduction upon DOM-B depletion (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), while H2A.V mRNA level was unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Among the interactors, only RNAi against the DOM-B.C-specific subunit ARP6 reduced H2A.V levels to a similar extent as DOM-B knock-down.
source: Among the interactors found in our mass-spectrometry analysis, only RNAi against the DOM-B.C-specific subunit ARP6 reduced H2A.V levels to a similar extent (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: H2A.V was not affected by the knock-down of DOM-A, TIP60 or other DOM-A.C-specific subunits.
source: H2A.V was not affected by the knock-down of DOM-A, TIP60 or other DOM-A.C-specific subunits (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C,D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C,D

claim: ChIP-seq revealed dramatic effects on H2A.V levels along the entire genome upon depletion of DOM-B, including promoters and transcriptional termination sites.
source: As expected, we scored dramatic effects on H2A.V levels along the entire genome upon depletion of DOM-B, including promoters and transcriptional termination sites (Figure 3B,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3B,C

claim: Depletion of DOM-A did not affect chromosomal H2A.V at promoters or transcriptional termination sites.
source: Depletion of DOM-A did not affect chromosomal H2A.V at any of these sites (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3B,C

claim: Wild-type DOM-B transgene rescued H2A.V levels in complementation assay.
source: We detected higher levels of H2A.V in cells complemented with a wild-type DOM-B transgene, indicating the expected rescue (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The remodeling-defective mutant DOM-B transgene (K945G) did not increase the residual H2A.V levels.
source: Conversely, the remodeling-defective mutant transgene did not increase the residual H2A.V levels (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3F

claim: Only the wild-type DOM-B could restore H2A.V levels in complementation assay.
source: Comparing the mean H2A.V signal between cells that express the transgene (GFP+) and cells that don't (GFP-), revealed once more that only the wild-type could restore H2A.V levels (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 3G

claim: The DOM-B.C is responsible for the incorporation of H2A.V in an ATP-dependent manner.
source: The data suggest that the DOM-B.C is responsible for the incorporation of H2A.V in an ATP-dependent manner.
evidence: Inferred from complementation assays showing ATP-dependence

claim: The core NuA4.C subunit EAF1 is a small protein with prominent N-terminal HSA and C-terminal SANT domains.
source: The core NuA4.C subunit EAF1 is a small protein with prominent N-terminal HSA and C-terminal SANT domains.
evidence: Based on known structure of yeast NuA4 complex

claim: DOM-A features HSA and SANT domains separated by the long ATPase domain.
source: DOM-A also features similarly arranged domains, but they are separated by the long ATPase domain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by domain structure comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: RNAi against DOM-A, but not against DOM-B, specifically reduces H4K12ac (average 28.9% reduction) and, to a lesser extent, H4K5ac (average 23.1% reduction).
source: Our analysis showed that RNAi against DOM-A, but not against DOM-B, specifically reduces H4K12ac (average 28.9% reduction) and, to a lesser extent, H4K5ac (average 23.1% reduction) (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by targeted mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Depletion of TIP60 reduces H4K12ac by on average 36.3% and H4K5ac by 16.4%.
source: Importantly, unsupervised clustering shows that depleting DOM-A or TIP60 lead to very similar changes in histone acetylation patterns: depletion of TIP60 also reduces H4K12ac, by on average 36.3% and H4K5ac by 16.4% (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by targeted mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Depleting DOM-A or TIP60 lead to very similar changes in histone acetylation patterns.
source: Importantly, unsupervised clustering shows that depleting DOM-A or TIP60 lead to very similar changes in histone acetylation patterns: depletion of TIP60 also reduces H4K12ac, by on average 36.3% and H4K5ac by 16.4% (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: DOM depletion causes a decrease in monomethylation and increase of trimethylation at H3K27, a bit stronger for DOM-A or TIP60.
source: Interestingly, we detected a decrease in monomethylation and increase of trimethylation at H3K27 by DOM depletion, a bit stronger for DOM-A or TIP60 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by targeted mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: H4 methylation was unchanged upon DOM depletion.
source: H4 methylation was unchanged (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by targeted mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: H4K12ac signal was reduced in many regions of the genome, including promoters and transcriptional termination sites, upon TIP60 RNAi and to a lesser extent upon DOM-A RNAi.
source: We found the H4K12ac signal reduced in many regions of the genome, including promoters and transcriptional termination sites, upon TIP60 RNAi and to a lesser extent upon DOM-A RNAi (Figure 4B,C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F,H,I), but the results suffer from variability, probably due to a low ChIP efficiency of the H4K12ac antibody (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B,C

claim: Genes downregulated in DOM-A or TIP60 knock-down tend to have higher basal levels of H4K12ac at promoters.
source: Comparison between H4K12ac and transcription showed that genes downregulated in DOM-A or TIP60 knock-down tend to have higher basal levels of H4K12ac at promoters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by composite plot analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G

claim: The reduction of H4K12ac by DOM-A or TIP60 knock-down is global and does not affect some genes specifically.
source: The reduction of H4K12ac by DOM-A or TIP60 knock-down, however, is global and does not affect some genes specifically (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by violin-boxplot analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H

claim: Depletion of DOM-B caused an unexpected increase in H4K12 acetylation at many chromosomal regions that lose the mark upon DOM-A ablation.
source: Remarkably, depletion of DOM-B caused an unexpected increase in H4K12 acetylation at many chromosomal regions that lose the mark upon DOM-A ablation (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B,C

claim: Depletion of H2A.V causes a small H4K12ac increase similarly to DOM-B knock-down.
source: Depletion of H2A.V also causes a small H4K12ac increase similarly to DOM-B knock-down, as if the absence of this remodeler and/or its substrate allowed more DOM-A activity at promoters.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B,C

claim: The wild-type DOM-A transgene restored H4K12 acetylation in complementation assay.
source: As expected, the wild-type DOM-A transgene restored H4K12 acetylation (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D

claim: H4K12 acetylation by DOM-A.C did not depend on a functional DOM-A ATPase.
source: Remarkably, this acetylation did not depend on a functional DOM-A ATPase.
evidence: Supported by complementation assay showing mutant DOM-A can restore H4K12ac

claim: Both the wild-type and the mutant DOM-A transgenes could restore H4K12ac levels.
source: Comparison of the mean H4K12ac signals in cells that do or do not express the transgene confirmed that both, the wild-type and the mutant transgenes, could restore H4K12ac levels (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 4E

claim: A DOM.C was previously reported after overexpression and affinity-purification of tagged PONTIN.
source: A DOM.C was previously reported after overexpression and affinity-purification of tagged PONTIN (Kusch et al., 2004), which yielded a mixture of DOM-A and DOM-B complexes and may be contaminated with the dINO80 complex, which also contains PONTIN (Klymenko et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: DOM-B affects H2A.V levels during fly oogenesis.
source: We previously showed that DOM-B, and not DOM-A or TIP60, affects H2A.V levels during fly oogenesis (Börner and Becker, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: ARP6 is necessary for the maintenance of H2A.V global levels, just like DOM-B.
source: We also discovered a previously unidentified subunit, ARP6, which is necessary for the maintenance of H2A.V global levels, just like DOM-B.
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing H2A.V reduction upon ARP6 knock-down

claim: In yeast SWR1.C and human SRCAP.C, the ARP6 orthologs are indispensable for nucleosome remodeling since they couple the ATPase motor to productive nucleosome sliding.
source: In yeast SWR1.C and human SRCAP.C, the ARP6 orthologs are indispensable for nucleosome remodeling since they couple the ATPase motor to productive nucleosome sliding (Matsuda et al., 2010; Willhoft et al., 2018; Willhoft and Wigley, 2020; Wu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: The Drosophila DOM-B.C is likely to employ a similar remodeling mechanism to yeast SWR1.C.
source: The Drosophila DOM-B.C is likely to employ a similar remodeling mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from similarity to yeast SWR1.C and presence of ARP6

claim: Knock-down of DOM-B affects transcription, but the effects overlap only partially with those that follow H2A.V depletion.
source: Knock-down of DOM-B affects transcription, but the effects overlap only partially with those that follow H2A.V depletion.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq correlation analysis

claim: The reduction of H2A.V levels upon DOM-B knock-down is not as extensive as the one caused by direct depletion of H2A.V.
source: First, the reduction of H2A.V levels upon DOM-B knock-down is not as extensive as the one caused by direct depletion of H2A.V.
evidence: Inferred from western blot and ChIP-seq data

claim: The residual levels of H2A.V upon DOM-B depletion may suffice to regulate transcription at many promoters.
source: The residual levels of H2A.V upon DOM-B depletion may suffice to regulate transcription at many promoters.
evidence: Speculative explanation for partial overlap in transcriptional effects

claim: DOM-B.C may impact transcription independently of H2A.V incorporation.
source: Second, we cannot exclude that DOM-B.C also impacts transcription independently of H2A.V incorporation.
evidence: Speculative explanation for transcriptional effects

claim: The global increase of H4K12ac at promoters upon DOM-B knock-down might indirectly compensate for the loss of H2A.V at some specific genes.
source: Third, the global increase of H4K12ac at promoters upon DOM-B knock-down might indirectly compensate for the loss of H2A.V at some specific genes.
evidence: Speculative explanation for transcriptional effects

claim: DOM-A.C did not affect H2A.V incorporation under physiological conditions in any assays.
source: The DOM-A.C, surprisingly, did not affect H2A.V incorporation under physiological conditions in any of our assays, in agreement with what has been observed for the DOM-A isoform during oogenesis (Börner and Becker, 2016).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and western blot data, and citation to previous work

claim: DOM-A.C lacks the ARP6 subunit that is a mechanistic requirement for nucleosome remodeling by INO80-type remodelers.
source: DOM-A.C lacks the ARP6 subunit that is a mechanistic requirement for nucleosome remodeling by INO80-type remodelers (Willhoft and Wigley, 2020).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data and citation to previous work

claim: The ATPase domain of DOM-A is identical to the one in DOM-B.
source: Because the ATPase domain of DOM-A is identical to the one in DOM-B, it is possible that DOM-A utilizes ATP under circumstances that we did not monitor in our study.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: It is possible that DOM-A utilizes ATP under circumstances not monitored in this study.
source: Because the ATPase domain of DOM-A is identical to the one in DOM-B, it is possible that DOM-A utilizes ATP under circumstances that we did not monitor in our study.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential DOM-A ATPase activity

claim: DOM-A.C-specific subunits may have an inhibitory effect on DOM-A ATPase activity through allosteric regulation.
source: It is also possible that DOM-A.C-specific subunits have an inhibitory effect on DOM-A ATPase activity through allosteric regulation.
evidence: Speculative explanation for lack of ATPase activity

claim: The recombinant human ortholog of DOM-A, EP400, can incorporate H2A.Z.
source: Of note, the recombinant human ortholog of DOM-A, EP400, can incorporate H2A.Z (Park et al., 2010), but H2A.Z levels are unaffected if EP400 is depleted in vivo, where it resides in a multi-subunit complex (Pradhan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: H2A.Z levels are unaffected if EP400 is depleted in vivo, where it resides in a multi-subunit complex.
source: Of note, the recombinant human ortholog of DOM-A, EP400, can incorporate H2A.Z (Park et al., 2010), but H2A.Z levels are unaffected if EP400 is depleted in vivo, where it resides in a multi-subunit complex (Pradhan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Regulation of nucleosome remodeling through autoinhibitory domains or associated subunits is a widespread mechanism.
source: Regulation of nucleosome remodeling through autoinhibitory domains or associated subunits is a widespread mechanism (Clapier et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: The DOM-A.C is the functional equivalent of the yeast NuA4.C, which acetylates the H4 N-terminus.
source: Our data suggest that the DOM-A.C is the functional equivalent of the yeast NuA4.C, which acetylates the H4 N-terminus (Kuo et al., 2015) and possibly other proteins.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data and citation to previous work

claim: Depletion of DOM-A.C causes a significant reduction of H4K12ac at a global level.
source: Depletion of DOM-A.C causes a significant reduction of H4K12ac at a global level.
evidence: Supported by targeted mass spectrometry and ChIP-seq data

claim: Additional acetyltransferases such as CHAMEAU may target H4K12.
source: Some genomic regions that still retain a high H4K12ac ChIP signal in the absence of DOM-A may be explained by the presence of additional acetyltransferases targeting H4K12, such as CHAMEAU (Feller et al., 2015; Peleg et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: H4K12ac has been implicated in aging.
source: The function of H4K12ac is still largely unknown in Drosophila, although it has been implicated in aging (Peleg et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: H4K12ac may participate in transcriptional regulation since knock-down of DOM-A or TIP60 perturb the transcriptional program in a very similar manner.
source: We speculate that H4K12ac may participate in transcriptional regulation since knock-down of DOM-A or TIP60 perturb the transcriptional program in a very similar manner.
evidence: Speculative statement based on correlation between DOM-A/TIP60 knock-down effects

claim: H4K12ac is the most abundant H4 acetylation.
source: Given that H4K12ac is the most abundant H4 acetylation (Feller et al., 2015; Peleg et al., 2016), we also cannot exclude that some of these effects are due to global and aberrant chromosomal condensation.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: H2A-containing nucleosomes may be a better substrate for the DOM-A.C compared to the ones containing only H2A.V.
source: It is possible that H2A-containing nucleosomes are a better substrate for the DOM-A.C compared to the ones containing only H2A.V.
evidence: Speculative explanation for H4K12ac increase upon H2A.V depletion

claim: The loss of H2A.V might result in higher H4K12ac catalyzed by TIP60.
source: The loss of the variant might therefore result in higher H4K12ac catalyzed by TIP60.
evidence: Speculative explanation for H4K12ac increase upon H2A.V depletion

claim: In the absence of DOM-A, TIP60 is unstable suggesting that the DOM-A.C is the major form of TIP60, at least in D. melanogaster cells.
source: In the absence of DOM-A, TIP60 is unstable suggesting that the DOM-A.C is the major form of TIP60, at least in D. melanogaster cells.
evidence: Inferred from TIP60 protein reduction upon DOM-A knock-down

claim: During evolution a HAT module and some components of the SWR1.C became stably associated in a new functional complex, the dNuA4.C.
source: It also suggests that during evolution a HAT module and some components of the SWR1.C became stably associated in a new functional complex, the dNuA4.C, as it has been proposed for the human EP400 complex (Auger et al., 2008).
evidence: Inferred from composition of DOM-A.C and citation to previous work

claim: In C. albicans, acetylation of EAF1 by TIP60 mediates a reversible association between the NuA4.C and SWR1.C.
source: An intermediate case is found in C. albicans, where acetylation of EAF1 by TIP60 mediates a reversible association between the NuA4.C and SWR1.C (Wang et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Inserting the ATPase domain of the Drosophila DOM between the HSA and SANT domains of yeast EAF1 does not affect its function.
source: In yeast, inserting the ATPase domain of the Drosophila DOM between the HSA and SANT domains of EAF1, the central subunit of the yeast NuA4, does not affect its function (Auger et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: The transcription factor CG12054 has been found as a potential DOM partner in a previous screen.
source: Of those, the transcription factor CG12054 has been found as a potential DOM partner in a previous screen (Rhee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: The human ortholog of CG12054, JAZF1, appears to be involved in transcriptional repression.
source: Its human ortholog, JAZF1, appears to be involved in transcriptional repression (Nakajima et al., 2004) and has been associated to endometrial stromal tumors (Koontz et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: The function of CG12054 in flies is unknown.
source: Its function in flies is unknown.
evidence: Statement about lack of knowledge

claim: In yeast, the SWR1 and NuA4 complexes are entirely separate entities.
source: In yeast, the SWR1 and NuA4 complexes are entirely separate entities.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of yeast chromatin complexes

claim: In humans, the paralogous SRCAP and EP400 protein ATPases each organize different complexes that may serve distinct, conserved functions.
source: In humans, whose genomes underwent duplication events, the paralogous SRCAP and EP400 protein ATPases each organize different complexes that may serve distinct, conserved functions.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of human chromatin complexes

claim: The gene orthologs of dom in honeybee, jewel wasp, Jerdon's jumping ant, red flour beetle and common house spider undergo alternative splicing to generate at least two isoforms with different C-termini.
source: Surprisingly, the gene orthologs of dom in honeybee (A. mellifera, LOC413341), jewel wasp (N. vitripennis, LOC100115939), Jerdon's jumpin ant (H. saltator, LOC105183375), red flour beetle (T. castaneum, LOC656538) and even in the common house spider (P. tepidariorum, LOC107448208) undergo alternative splicing to generate at least two isoforms with different C-termini.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis of orthologs

claim: The mode of specification of SWR1 and NuA4 through splice variants might be more wide-spread throughout the Arthropoda phylum.
source: The mode of specification of SWR1 and NuA4 through splice variants might therefore not be limited to Drosophila, but more wide-spread throughout the Arthropoda phylum.
evidence: Inferred from conservation of alternative splicing in dom orthologs

claim: H2A.Z accounts for ~5–10% of the total H2A-type histone pool in vertebrates.
source: The very conserved H2A variant H2A.Z accounts for ~5–10% of the total H2A-type histone pool in vertebrates (Redon et al., 2002; Thatcher and Gorovsky, 1994) and flies (Bonnet et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work
